key_terms.meaning: A device that converts a physical quantity (temperature, pressure, speed) into an electrical signal the ECU can read.
The circuit block that amplifies, filters and scales a raw sensor output into the 0–5 V range an ADC can accept.
Analog-to-digital converter; turns a continuous voltage into a number with a fixed number of steps, e.g. a 10-bit ADC on a 5 V reference gives 5/1024 ≈ 4.9 mV per step.
Active sensors need an excitation supply (potentiometer, Hall IC); passive sensors generate their own signal (thermocouple, piezoelectric knock sensor).
Absolute pressure is measured against vacuum; relative (gauge) pressure is measured against ambient, so absolute = gauge + atmospheric.
Accuracy is closeness to the true value; drift is a slow change of output over time or temperature with the input held constant.
A Wheatstone bridge is four resistances fed by an excitation voltage; a small change in one arm produces a small differential voltage that is then amplified.
A correction added to a thermocouple reading, because the thermocouple measures the difference between the hot junction and the cooler reference junction.
A heated wire in the intake stream is held at constant temperature; the current needed to keep it hot rises with air mass flow and becomes the flow signal.
Manifold absolute pressure sensor; a silicon diaphragm with piezoresistive strain gauges gives a voltage proportional to absolute intake pressure.
A gap in the crankshaft target wheel that produces a unique pulse so the ECU can identify top dead centre of cylinder one.
A coil and magnet facing a toothed wheel; each tooth passage generates an AC pulse whose amplitude and frequency rise with speed.
A current-carrying semiconductor in a magnetic field develops a small transverse voltage; a Hall IC switches cleanly when a shutter or magnet passes.
An LED and phototransistor pair with a slotted disc between them; each slot gives a digital pulse and a second offset track gives direction.
Negative temperature coefficient resistor: resistance falls steeply and non-linearly as temperature rises, used for coolant, intake air and cabin air.
The chemically correct air-fuel mass ratio; about 14.7 kg of air per kg of petrol, giving lambda = 1.
A solid-electrolyte cell that produces a voltage when oxygen on its two sides differs; output is a switch around lambda = 1 for the narrowband type.
A ceramic disc bolted to the block that produces a charge when the block vibrates, letting the ECU detect detonation and retard spark.
A solenoid converts coil current into a straight pull; a stepper motor turns in fixed angular steps as its coils are energised in sequence.
Battery state of charge is estimated by integrating measured current over time; SOC is the remaining charge as a fraction of rated capacity.

takeaways: Every sensor chain ends at the ECU as a voltage or a pulse, so signal conditioning and the ADC set the resolution and accuracy you can actually use.
Air charge is measured either directly by a mass air flow sensor or indirectly by a MAP sensor with speed density; the choice changes the fuel calculation.
Crankshaft position sensing must give both angle and speed, and the missing-tooth reference is what fixes cylinder one to top dead centre.
Hall, variable reluctance and optical sensors are all non-contact, so they avoid the wear of a rubbing contact and give a digital pulse.
The oxygen sensor closes the fuel loop: it does not measure fuel, it measures the result and the ECU trims the injection quantity from it.
Knock and angular-rate sensors feed protection and stability functions, not fuel metering, and they work on vibration rather than steady values.
Actuators are the output side of the ECU, and almost all of them are driven by switched current: solenoid, relay, stepper or PWM motor drive.
Battery current and voltage sensing turn a chemical store into numbers the BMS can act on, giving SOC, state of health and state of function.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to draw the sensor, its conditioning circuit and the ECU input as one block diagram, then explain how a wrong signal changes fuel, spark or actuator action and what the driver sees.

bank.q: Define a sensor and classify automotive sensors by the quantity measured, by active or passive nature, and by contact or non-contact operation. Explain the signal conditioning chain from sensor to ADC.
outline: Definition: physical quantity to electrical signal
Classification: position, speed, pressure, flow, temperature, gas concentration, torque, vibration
Active needs excitation; passive self-generating
Contact wears; non-contact (Hall, optical, inductive) does not
Conditioning: protection, excitation, bridge, amplify, filter (low-pass anti-alias), scale to ADC range
ADC resolution example: 10-bit on 5 V reference gives about 4.9 mV per step

bank.q: Describe the construction and working of a hot-wire mass air flow sensor and a piezoresistive MAP sensor. State the advantages and limits of each.
outline: Hot wire: heated element in intake, constant-temperature bridge, current is the flow signal
Hot film and compensation element for air temperature
Needs burn-off cycle after shut-down to clean the wire
MAP: silicon diaphragm, diffused piezoresistive gauges, Wheatstone bridge, absolute pressure
MAP used in speed-density fuel calculation with engine speed and intake air temperature
Limits: MAF sensitive to dirt and backflow pulsation; MAP needs a barometric reference for altitude

bank.q: Explain how the crankshaft angular position and engine speed are sensed, and how the ECU uses the reference mark for ignition and fuel timing.
outline: Target wheel on crank pulley or flywheel, tooth count sets angular resolution
Missing tooth or extra tooth gives a unique reference pulse at a known angle before top dead centre
Speed from pulse frequency, angle from pulse count since reference
Variable reluctance gives an AC signal; Hall gives a square wave
ECU calculates ignition advance and injection start angle from angle and speed
Also drives the tachometer and the stall detection

bank.q: State the Hall effect and describe a Hall-effect position sensor and an optical crankshaft position sensor with their output waveforms.
outline: Hall voltage is transverse to current and magnetic field, proportional to flux density
Hall IC adds a comparator and output stage, giving a clean square wave
Magnet and vane or shutter arrangement across the air gap
Optical: LED, slotted or windowed disc, phototransistor
Two tracks 90 degrees apart give direction and finer resolution
Both are non-contact, so no wear, but optical is sensitive to dirt and oil mist

bank.q: Describe throttle position sensing with a potentiometer and coolant temperature sensing with an NTC thermistor, including the 5 V reference and voltage divider.
outline: Potentiometer: three wires, 5 V reference, ground, wiper voltage proportional to angle
Two-track potentiometers for plausibility checking
Idle and wide-open-throttle switch contacts in older types
NTC: resistance falls with temperature, non-linear, so the ECU uses a lookup table
Divider formula: Vout = 5 x R_thermistor / (R_thermistor + R_pullup)
Fail-safe values: throttle default, coolant default for cold start

bank.q: Explain the working of the exhaust gas oxygen sensor and how it closes the fuel loop. Compare narrowband and wideband types.
outline: Zirconia electrolyte conducts oxygen ions above about 300 degrees Celsius
Nernst voltage switches sharply around lambda = 1; heater brings it up to temperature fast
Narrowband: switch output about 0.1 V lean to 0.9 V rich
Wideband: pumping cell with a reference, current proportional to lambda over a wide range
ECU short-term and long-term fuel trim from the sensor signal
Closed loop only after the sensor is hot; open loop at start and full load

bank.q: Describe a piezoelectric knock sensor and an angular-rate sensor, and state how the ECU uses each signal.
outline: Knock: detonation gives block vibration in a characteristic frequency band
Piezoelectric ceramic produces charge proportional to acceleration; charge amplifier converts it
ECU windows the signal after each spark and compares with a threshold
Action: retard spark on the knocking cylinder, then gradually restore advance
Angular rate: vibrating element or MEMS gyroscope giving yaw rate voltage
Used with wheel speed and steering angle for stability control

bank.q: Explain solenoid, relay and stepper motor actuators in automotive use, with one circuit each for a fuel injector, a relay-driven load and an idle air stepper.
outline: Solenoid: coil pulls plunger, force rises with current, flow area set by pulse width
Injector: peak-and-hold or saturated drive, flyback diode, pulse width sets fuel quantity
Relay: small coil current switches a large load current, coil driven by low-side switch
Stepper: two coils, sequence of steps moves the pintle, no feedback needed, position held by detent
PWM drive for proportional solenoid valves such as EGR and VVT
Failures: open coil, shorted coil, sticking plunger

bank.q: Describe current and voltage measurement in a battery management system and explain how state of charge, state of health and state of function are estimated.
outline: Current: shunt resistor with differential amplifier, or Hall or fluxgate clamp for isolation
Voltage: resistive divider into ADC, per cell and pack level, isolation barrier
Coulomb counting: charge = integral of current over time
SOC from coulomb counting with a model correction at rest, and open-circuit voltage lookup
SOH from capacity fade and internal resistance rise
SOF from available power at present SOC and temperature

bank.q: A crankshaft target wheel has 36 teeth with one tooth missing and runs at 3000 rev/min. Calculate the pulses per revolution, the crank angle per pulse, the pulse frequency and the time between pulses. Explain how a single missed pulse is detected as the reference.
outline: Pulses per revolution = 35
Crank angle per pulse = 360/36 = 10 degrees
Pulse frequency = 35 x 3000/60 = 1750 Hz
Time between pulses = 1/1750 s ≈ 0.57 ms
Missed pulse gives a gap of twice the normal interval
Reference angle placed a fixed number of degrees before top dead centre

bank.q: An NTC coolant sensor forms a voltage divider with a 2.2 kilo-ohm pull-up to a 5 V reference and feeds a 10-bit ADC. For a sensor resistance of 2.2 kilo-ohm, find the divider voltage and the ADC count. State one practical problem with this arrangement.
outline: Vout = 5 x R_t/(R_t + R_pullup) = 5 x 2.2/4.4 = 2.5 V
ADC step = 5/1024 ≈ 4.9 mV
Sensor is non-linear, so counts must be mapped through a lookup table
Self-heating error if pull-up current is too large; wire resistance adds error

bank.q: An engine sets a lean fuel trim code at idle only, with normal behaviour at cruise. Using air flow, manifold pressure, throttle position and oxygen sensor readings, outline the step-by-step diagnosis and the measurement you would take at each step.
outline: Confirm with fuel trim data, both short term and long term
Check for unmetered air: intake leaks after the MAF, vacuum hoses, PCV, brake booster
Compare MAF reading with expected value from engine size and speed at idle
Compare MAP at idle with the specified vacuum, and check the barometric reading at key-on
Check throttle position at closed throttle for a correct idle voltage
Read the oxygen sensor switching rate and check for a lazy or biased sensor
Check fuel pressure and injector flow before condemning a sensor

bank.q: Compare Hall-effect, variable reluctance and optical sensors for crankshaft position sensing in a hot, oily engine bay. Analyse failure modes and explain how the ECU can limp home when the signal is lost.
outline: VR: no supply needed, robust, but output falls to zero at very low speed and amplitude varies with speed
Hall: needs supply, works down to zero speed, gives a constant square wave, sensitive to supply and ground faults
Optical: best resolution, but oil mist and dirt block the light path
Failure modes: open coil, shorted turns, air-gap change, metal debris on the magnet, connector corrosion
Limp home: substitute cam sensor signal, or fixed timing and speed-density fuel, or default to a fixed advance
Diagnosis: check supply, ground, signal with a scope at cranking

bank.q: Evaluate the choice between a narrowband and a wideband oxygen sensor for a petrol engine that must meet close-coupled catalyst light-off and lean-burn operation. Support your answer with the control strategy each sensor allows.
outline: Narrowband: cheap, sharp switch at lambda = 1, only useful for holding stoichiometric
Cannot measure individual cylinder or lean-burn deviation with accuracy
Wideband: pump cell, current proportional to lambda, range roughly lambda 0.7 to air
Enables catalyst heating strategy, individual cylinder trim, lean-burn and ethanol blend adaptation
Needs heater control and a reference air supply, higher cost
Evaluate: emissions benefit and fuel saving against cost and durability of the pump cell

bank.q: A vehicle reports a random misfire under load with no stored sensor fault. Evaluate how knock, crankshaft position, oxygen and acceleration sensors together let the ECU detect and respond to the fault, and state which signals you would capture first.
outline: Crank sensor pulse timing shows the speed drop of the misfiring cylinder
Cam and crank correlation confirms the cylinder identity
Oxygen sensor sees the unburnt oxygen pulse, catalyst damage risk
Knock sensor separates detonation from a plain misfire
Acceleration or roughness measurement from crank speed variation
Response: retard spark, reduce boost, cut that injector, flash the MIL
First captures: crank and cam signals with a scope, then fuel trim and misfire counter data

glossary.def: A device that turns an electrical command from the ECU into mechanical movement or flow.
How close a measured value is to the true value, usually quoted as a percentage of full scale or an absolute value.
The smallest change in input that the sensor and ADC can distinguish, set by bit count and reference voltage.
The change in output for a unit change in input, for example millivolts per kilopascal for a MAP sensor.
How closely the sensor output follows a straight line against input over its working range.
The difference in output when the same input is reached from increasing and from decreasing direction.
A circuit or routine that removes unwanted frequency content, such as a low-pass filter to reject ignition noise before the ADC.
Pressure measured with vacuum as the zero reference, so it never goes negative.
Pressure measured relative to the surrounding atmosphere, so it can be positive or negative.
Four resistances in a diamond, excited by a supply, giving a near-zero output at balance and a small differential voltage when one arm changes.
A semiconductor resistor whose resistance changes strongly with temperature; NTC types fall in resistance as temperature rises.
Two dissimilar metals joined at a hot junction, producing a small voltage proportional to the temperature difference between junctions.
Resistance temperature detector, usually platinum, with a small and nearly linear positive resistance change with temperature.
The ratio of actual air-fuel ratio to the stoichiometric ratio; lambda = 1 means chemically correct.
The percentage correction the ECU applies to injection quantity from oxygen sensor feedback; short term is fast, long term is learned.
Abnormal rapid burning of the end gas in the cylinder, producing a pressure spike and high-frequency block vibration.
Exhaust gas recirculation valve; a solenoid or stepper or vacuum-operated valve that admits exhaust into the intake to lower combustion temperature and NOx.
An electromagnetic valve that opens for a commanded time to spray a measured fuel quantity.
An electromagnetically operated switch that lets a small ECU current control a large load current.
A diode across an inductive load that gives the collapsing coil current a path, protecting the driving switch.
Battery management system; the electronics that measures cell voltage, current and temperature and estimates SOC, SOH and SOF.
Remaining charge in a battery as a percentage of its rated capacity.
The present capacity and internal resistance of an aged battery compared with its new condition.
The power the battery can actually deliver or accept now, at the present charge and temperature.
An angular-rate sensor, usually vibrating MEMS, whose output voltage is proportional to rotation rate about an axis.
Light detection and ranging; a pulsed laser and detector that measures distance to objects from time of flight, used in driver assistance.
